title: AIDC Power Conversion — The 800 VDC Race
topic: Who is winning the AI data-centre power-conversion transition, layer by layer — silicon, the rack, the sidecar and hall-edge block, and the facility and grid tier

scope.rationale: The covered NVIDIA 800 VDC roster, cut by layer rather than as one peer family, plus Power Electronics. Sixteen dossiers across four layers: silicon and the last centimetre (infineon, vicor); the rack — shelves, PSUs, BBUs (delta-electronics, liteon, megmeet, flex); the sidecar and the hall-edge block, TRU and SST (zhonhen, sungrow, sinexcel, power-electronics, with delta-electronics again); and the facility and grid tier (vertiv, eaton, schneider-electric, abb, ge-vernova, hitachi-energy). Ten are named on NVIDIA's own published 800 VDC rosters; the other six (vicor, zhonhen, sungrow, sinexcel, schneider-electric, power-electronics) are in because the corpus holds substantive 800 VDC records for them, not because NVIDIA lists them. The like-for-like rule is met within each layer's table rather than across the report. power-electronics was added at the 2026-09-25 rev2 re-run for AIPCS, its medium-voltage-to-800 VDC unit. huawei-digital-power is covered but out of scope because sanctions fence it from the ecosystem assessed; mitsubishi-electric is a candidate for the next edition; the venture SST set is scored in the 23 September SST report.

gaps: huawei-digital-power is covered but excluded from scope: sanctions place it outside the NVIDIA/US ecosystem this report assesses. Its dossier is cited once, for the FCC action, which bears on the whole roster rather than on Huawei.

mitsubishi-electric is covered and belongs to the conversion stack but is outside this scope; it is a candidate for the next edition. power-electronics, in scope from this edition, is private: its revenue is company-stated and unaudited, and no AIPCS order, customer or input voltage class is published. The 8 September edition wrongly described both as carrying no dossier.
heron-power, amperesand, dg-matrix, novos-power and siemens-energy are covered and scored in sst-hall-edge-block-rev2--competitive--2026-09-23; not re-scored here.

The Option A/B/C slot definitions and the TRU-now / SST-2029 timing frame come from internal research on NVIDIA's white papers (the Industry Guidance NVIDIA module), not from dossier citations — passages leaning on them are marked as analysis.

The normalized-KPI overlay covers whole-company revenue only, and fiscal years differ across the set (Infineon's FY2025 ended 30 September 2025; Flex's FY2026 ended 31 March 2026; Hitachi Energy's FY2025 ended 31 March 2026). No company in the set discloses an audited AI-data-centre power-conversion revenue line, so no share-of-market table is possible from dossier data.
Delta, LITEON and Megmeet share and rank figures are trade and brokerage estimates (WAWT, Soochow, TrendForce, KGI), not company disclosures.

bluf: BOTTOM LINE UP FRONT: Seventeen days on, the four-layer picture holds, and the one thing that moved is the rack's order of play — which the corpus can now state rather than flag as contested. Delta leads, LITEON is second, and Megmeet is a qualified third source: late on GB200 by its own account, in batch orders on GB300, and placed third by the only 2026 research that ranks it; the story that it displaced LITEON traces to early-2025 pieces that label it rumour. The hall edge still has exactly one covered vendor whose filing says a solid-state transformer is supplying the market, Sungrow — but its own curve is small-batch trials through 2026 and batch orders from 2027, so no vendor in this report sells an SST at volume yet, and Megmeet's is in pre-research with no disclosed voltage class and, on the company's word, no volume sales for two to three years. For a first week at Megmeet the usable read is three lines: the defensible position is the rack and the 380–480 VAC sidecar, where power products grew 60.92% in H1 on an expanding margin; the defensible NVIDIA claim is list membership, not rank; and the Q3 report due by 31 October is the first test of a full-year consensus that needs roughly RMB 535M of profit in the second half against RMB 252M in the first.

keyJudgments.text: We assess Delta remains the benchmark the rack layer is measured against, and the revised corpus strengthens the claim on magnitude without converting it into a disclosure. WAWT puts Delta #1 in NVIDIA AI-server power [c:c7]; Soochow (April 2026) estimates Delta above 70% of NVIDIA's 2025 power supply [c:c56]; TrendForce names it the primary beneficiary of the 800 V HVDC shift with first volume shipments called for 3Q26 [c:c8]; and it publishes the deepest 800 VDC architecture in the set, from 660 kW in-row racks with embedded BBU [c:c9] up to a medium-voltage front end [c:c57]. Every share figure is a research-house or trade estimate.

We assess the rack layer's order of play is Delta, then LITEON, then Megmeet — and that the prior edition's 'contested narrative' framing can now be replaced with a sourced statement. Megmeet told investors in April 2026 that it was late on GB200 and won limited orders there, then won GB300 batch orders [c:c32]; Soochow expects it to become the third NVL72 PSU source after Delta and LITEON [c:c33]; TrendForce (March 2026) names Delta and LITEON the leading suppliers and says Megmeet's share will take time to build [c:c58][c:c34]; and the contemporaneous January 2025 supplier account names LITEON second [c:c55]. The 'Megmeet displaced LITEON at #2' claim traces to two early-2025 pieces that label it market rumour [c:c35][c:c36], and the company declined to confirm it when asked directly [c:c37]. No independent 2026 NVIDIA power-shelf share table exists in the record, which is why this stays moderate.

We assess Megmeet's defensible position is the rack and the sidecar, and that it is measurably growing there. The H1 2026 interim reports power products up 60.92% to RMB 1.841B with gross margin up 2.62 points to 25.06% — the only one of the company's three largest segments whose margin expanded [c:c27]. Its NVIDIA standing is membership of a list: the interim calls it one of NVIDIA's designated recommended data-centre power suppliers [c:c27], the company's reply to the exchange's inquiry defines that as a place on the list NVIDIA recommends to its downstream customers [c:c38], and NVIDIA's own October 2025 post lists it among power-system components rather than in the data-centre power-systems tier where the medium-voltage vendors sit [c:c39]. No AI-data-centre revenue line is disclosed at any granularity [c:c27].

We assess Megmeet's solid-state transformer is an option on the later part of the decade rather than a product, on the company's own record. It was described as in pre-research (预研) on the May 2026 earnings call [c:c40]; in August the company said SST demand will not ramp for one to two years and that sales for the next two to three years will come from its existing product matrix [c:c41]; and no service-voltage class appears in the FY2025 annual report [c:c44], the HKEX application proof [c:c43] or the investor-relations records. The one press report of a '10 kV domestic / 35 kV overseas' plan [c:c42] is attributed to the May call, whose exchange-filed record contains no kV figure [c:c40]. This matches the 23 September SST report, which places Megmeet in the rack layer with an undisclosed option on the layer above.

We assess Sungrow holds a productised solid-state transformer and not yet a volume one, which tempers the prior edition's reading. Its H1 2026 interim describes EnerNeo as launched and supplying the market at 10–13.8 kV MVAC to 800 V DC, 1.5–4.5 MW, 98.5% [c:c15], and the 3 MW unit was launched publicly in July 2026 [c:c16]; its own commercialisation guidance is small-batch trials with lead customers through 2026, batch orders from 2027 and scale from 2028, and investor questions on North American hyperscaler sampling and UL certification went unanswered [c:c60]. It remains the only covered vendor with an exchange-filed 'supplying' statement for the device — first by a year on paper, not yet on volume.

We assess Zhonhen holds the widest gap in the corpus between architectural endorsement and disclosed commerce, and the H1 2026 interim widened rather than closed it. NVIDIA's August 2026 execution paper names the Panama Architecture as a transformer-rectifier implementation, yet the company's own 187-page interim contains no order, no backlog, no named customer, no capacity commitment and no occurrence of the words NVIDIA, SST or transformer-rectifier. Its data-centre power line nearly doubled to RMB 807.59M and carried more than the whole of group growth — at a gross margin falling 1.87 points, with operating cash flow at RMB −268.80M and the asset-liability ratio moving 40.83% to 47.97%. The growth is real and it is being bought.

We assess Sinexcel is pre-revenue in AI data-centre power on its own record rather than by inference. Management states across four separate post-results investor-relations records that AIDC critical-power products are samples in the development stage with formal sales not yet realised, and the string '800V' does not appear once in the 212-page interim. The AIDC-linked revenue that exists runs through power quality inside industrial supporting power, which grew 57.81% at a 61.94% margin — and management attributes the same AI build-out that drives it to the raw-material cost inflation compressing its charging margin by 4.43 points.

We assess the silicon layer's leverage is not proportional to its scale, and Vicor is the demonstration. It appears on no published NVIDIA roster, sells neither shelf nor block, and has whole-company revenue roughly one fortieth of Delta's — yet it converted its bus-converter patents into a February 2025 ITC exclusion order and then into royalties that reached a fifth of its June 2026 quarter. Infineon, by contrast, holds a strong named position among fourteen silicon providers, which is a good place to be and not a chokepoint.

We assess the facility and grid tier is hedging the same shrinking-UPS arithmetic in five different directions, and that the grid-tier members' real position is upstream of the contest this report scores. Vertiv leads on data-centre concentration and backlog, Eaton has bought adjacent scope, Schneider sells the reference design rather than the box, ABB is pushing UPS function up to 34.5 kV medium voltage, and GE Vernova and Hitachi Energy hold turbine slots and transformer capacity whose lead times set the energization date for every campus the rack vendors are selling into.

We assess CATL's move on Zhonhen reaches further into the listed company than the headline consideration implies, and that it was unconsummated at the Zhonhen dossier's 8 September pin. RMB 4,099,858,823.53 buys 49.00% of the controlling holdco — RMB 3.51bn cash plus CATL's own 49% of Times Tianyuan at RMB 588M — leaving the founders with 51% and, on the filing's account, no change of control. The shareholders' agreement nonetheless gives CATL a nominated director, a deputy general manager and the finance department manager of the listed company plus a parent-level quorum veto, locked for 60 months, in the same document that asserts no impact on independence in finance or personnel. Definitive documents were signed 2026-08-14 [c:c25].

sections.title: What changed since the 8 September edition
ps: **Three dossiers moved, all on 23 September, and the scope did not.** Megmeet was revised to profileVersion 8 on eighty-one sources, and the reconciliation that followed corrected Delta Electronics (v6) and LITEON (v7), which had carried the 'Megmeet displaced LITEON' claim as directionally corroborated. The other twelve dossiers are unchanged since the prior edition's pins. The four-layer cut is kept, with one addition: Power Electronics joins Layer 3, taking the scope to sixteen.

**The rank question is answered, and the answer is third.** The prior edition treated the #2 story as a contested narrative with no supporting source located. The revised record traces it to two early-2025 pieces that call it market rumour [c:c35][c:c36], shows the company declining to confirm it when asked in December 2024 [c:c37], and adds what the prior edition lacked: Megmeet's own account of being late on GB200 with limited orders before winning GB300 batch orders [c:c32], Soochow's expectation that it becomes the third NVL72 PSU source [c:c33], and TrendForce naming Delta and LITEON as the leading suppliers [c:c58]. Soochow's same note puts Delta above 70% of NVIDIA's 2025 power supply [c:c56] — a broker estimate, carried as one.

**Megmeet's commercial account is sharper and still unnamed.** The interim states batch delivery to 部分北美大客户 — some large North American customers — in H1 2026, with no customer named [c:c27]; a Goldman note relayed by Sina says the first GB300 volume order ran through a US-headquartered ODM [c:c45]. That reconciles the two corpus statements: there is volume, and there is no named reference win.

**Megmeet's solid-state transformer is dated on its own word.** Pre-research in May [c:c40]; in August, demand 'will not ramp for one to two years' and sales for two to three years from the existing product matrix [c:c41]. No voltage class appears in any filing. The prior edition's line that the SST was 'still in development' was right and understated the horizon.

**One correction to the prior edition's reading of an unchanged dossier.** The 8 September edition said Sungrow's SST was 'on the record as shipping'. The Sungrow dossier it pinned also carries the company's own curve — small-batch trials through 2026, batch orders from 2027, scale from 2028 [c:c60] — which that edition did not report. 'Supplying' is the filing's word [c:c15]; 'volume' is not yet anyone's.

**One correction to its limitations.** It stated that mitsubishi-electric and power-electronics carry no dossiers. Both were covered before that edition was written (Mitsubishi Electric from 4 September, Power Electronics from 6 September), and Power Electronics publishes AIPCS, a medium-voltage-to-800 V DC unit — a Layer 3 product. Power Electronics is added to Layer 3 in this edition; Mitsubishi Electric remains a candidate for the next one.

**Megmeet's corporate calendar moved in ways a newcomer will hear about.** On 22 September the board agreed to buy the 46.30% minority of its welding subsidiary for RMB 663.64M cash [c:c49]. The HKEX H-share application filed in June [c:c43] shows no hearing on the exchange's active-application list as of 23 September [c:c52]. Guosen cut its FY2026 profit forecast to RMB 652M after the half [c:c50], against a 15-institution consensus mean of RMB 787M [c:c51].

**Carried forward unchanged: the one regulatory prong that narrowed does not reach this roster.** The FCC's DA 26-870 modified the Covered List entry for foreign-produced power inverters, narrowing the test to UL 1741 utility-interactive inverters [c:c26]. No covered rack-power vendor in this report is reached by it — but the vendor this edition adds is: Power Electronics' dossier records that the test turns on where hardware is built, so its Spanish-built, SCADA-commanded storage inverters are covered, with US manufacturing as its stated answer [c:c66]. Whether AIPCS itself falls under the rule is not stated anywhere in the record.

**This edition supersedes the one published earlier on 25 September, the same day, for one reason: the scope addition.** Power Electronics publishes AIPCS, which converts medium-voltage AC to an 800 VDC bus in one enclosure [c:c61] — a Layer 3 product that neither the earlier 25 September edition nor the 23 September SST report scored. Nothing else in the earlier edition changed.

sections.title: Reading this with the 23 September SST hall-edge report
ps: **`sst-hall-edge-block-rev2--competitive--2026-09-23` stays current and this edition does not repeat it.** That report takes one layer — the medium-voltage-to-800 V DC hall-edge block — across eighteen vendors, adds the four venture SST companies (Heron Power, Amperesand, DG Matrix, Novos Power) and Siemens Energy, and scores them on the service-voltage class each has actually specified. Read it for Layer 3 in depth; read this edition for where the hall edge sits among the four layers.

**Where the two overlap they agree, because they pin the same dossiers.** Both pin Megmeet v8, Delta v6 and LITEON v7. Both place Megmeet at the rack and the sidecar with an undisclosed option on the layer above; both call its rack position a qualified third source; both treat Sungrow as the only covered vendor with an exchange-filed 'supplying' statement and add that its own curve puts batch orders in 2027. The SST report's sharper point — that the class hyperscale campuses take, 34.5 kV, is the class the one shipping-on-paper product (10–13.8 kV) cannot serve — is not restated here. That report does not score Power Electronics; this one does, in Layer 3.
**The earlier morning edition of 23 September is superseded by its rev2 and is not cited.**

sections.intro: Two covered vendors sit below every box in the chain. Like-for-like within the layer: both sell components into other people's shelves and blocks, and neither sells a rack.

sections.title: Whole-company scale — and why it does not rank the layer
sections.unit: USD millions, latest full fiscal year, normalized
sections.intro: The only figure the corpus can compare across all sixteen is whole-company revenue from the normalized-KPI overlay. It is a scale indicator, not a position in this race: no company in the set discloses an AI-data-centre power-conversion revenue line.
sections.note: Denominator: whole-company revenue for the latest full fiscal year in each dossier's normalized-KPI overlay, converted at the rate each dossier records. Fiscal years are not aligned — Infineon's FY2025 ended 30 September 2025, Flex's FY2026 ended 31 March 2026, Hitachi Energy's FY2025 ended 31 March 2026; the rest are calendar 2025. Read the ordering, not the gaps.

sections.title: Megmeet in this race — the first-week read
ps: **Say 'recommended supplier', not 'number two'.** The claim the record supports is the one the company itself makes: a place on the list NVIDIA recommends to its downstream customers [c:c38], in the power-system-components tier alongside Bizlink, Delta, Flex, Lead Wealth and LITEON [c:c39]. The rank claim that still circulates in trade conversation traces to rumour [c:c35][c:c36], the company would not confirm it [c:c37], and 2026 research puts Megmeet third [c:c33]. Repeating the #2 line to a customer who has read Soochow or TrendForce costs credibility that the true line does not.

**Lead with what the filing measures.** Power products grew 60.92% to RMB 1.841B in H1 2026, and its gross margin rose 2.62 points to 25.06% while the largest segment's fell [c:c27]. Direct overseas revenue grew about twice as fast as domestic [c:c27]. GB300 batch orders followed a late start on GB200 [c:c32], and batch delivery to some large North American customers began in the half, unnamed under NDA [c:c27]. That is a real, growing, margin-positive rack business, and it is the part of the company the filings can actually measure.

**Place the SST honestly.** The product line runs from shelf to sidecar to a converter above it, and everything below the converter is specified and shipping [c:c53][c:c54][c:c28]. The converter has no published input class [c:c43], is in pre-research [c:c40], and on the company's own dating will not sell in volume for two to three years [c:c41]. A customer's electrical engineer asks the input class early; the right answer today is that it is not yet published, and the sidecar takes the building's existing 380–480 VAC.

**Know what the Q3 report has to show.** H1 attributable profit was RMB 252.1M, of which RMB 133.9M was non-recurring; the 15-institution FY2026 consensus mean of RMB 787M implies about RMB 535M in H2 [c:c51], and Guosen has already cut to RMB 652M on competition and FX [c:c50]. The report is due by 31 October. The power-products line is the only proxy for the AI ramp, because no AI-data-centre revenue line exists to check it against [c:c27].

**Hold the US-footprint line carefully.** The company's website describes a 35,000 sq ft US manufacturing base in Richardson, Texas [c:c46], and a Texas licensing record shows a Megmeet fit-out there [c:c47]; the HKEX application proof lists no US manufacturing base among six [c:c43], and the Dallas test lab release does not say it sits on the same site [c:c48]. In a tariff or localisation conversation, the filed mitigation is Thailand, not Texas. At the hall edge, the covered vendor with the US story is Power Electronics — about 70% of FY2025 revenue from the United States [c:c63] and a Houston plant launching production in 2026 [c:c65] — which is the comparison a US buyer will reach for once Megmeet's converter has a class to quote.

sections.title: Four contests, not one — and only two of them are being won
ps: Separating the four layers is what makes the field legible: a vendor cannot lose the rack and win the hall, because the buyers, the qualification cycles and the incumbents differ at every level.

**Layer 1 (silicon) is not contested on volume — it is contested on position.** Infineon is one of fourteen named providers, which is a strong position and not a moat. Vicor is on no NVIDIA roster at all and is nonetheless the vendor with the most defensible economics in the report, because it converted an architectural claim into an ITC exclusion order and then into royalties. Scale does not predict leverage here: Vicor's whole-company revenue is roughly one fortieth of Delta's.

**Layer 2 (the rack) is the only layer with a settled leader, and its second and third places are now settled on the record too.** Delta is the benchmark on volume and portfolio depth. LITEON holds second on the research record and on US capacity commitments; Megmeet is third on the only 2026 ranking that names it, arrived late on GB200 and is growing into GB300. The contest that remains is not for second place — it is whether Megmeet's sidecar lead among mainland vendors turns into share as the architecture moves from shelves to side racks, which is a question for the Q3 and FY2026 filings rather than for trade reporting.

**Layer 3 (the hall-edge block) is where the prior edition's central judgment sits, and it survives with a correction of emphasis.** Every vendor here publishes or is developing a credible device. Only one — Sungrow — states in a filing that the device is supplying the market, and its own curve puts batch orders in 2027. The other two scoped vendors disclose either nothing at all (Zhonhen) or explicitly pre-commercial status (Sinexcel), and Megmeet's converter has no published class. Power Electronics, new to scope, publishes a transformer-based medium-voltage-to-800 VDC unit and, as a private company, no order record for it. Architectural validation and commercial inclusion remain separate questions; in this layer, nobody has yet answered the second at volume.

**Layer 4 (facility and grid) is contested on scope, not on the box.** All six incumbents face the same arithmetic — 800 VDC moves conversion toward the rack and shrinks the centralized UPS franchise — and each is hedging with something the rack vendors cannot sell: Vertiv with backlog and concentration, Eaton with acquired adjacent scope, Schneider with reference designs that set the procurement template, ABB with medium voltage, and GE Vernova and Hitachi Energy with the two genuinely scarce upstream resources, turbine slots and transformer capacity. The grid tier's constraint is not competitive position; it is delivery lead time, and it gates every layer beneath it.

**The cross-layer read.** The 800 VDC transition is still being won by vendors that already had the adjacent business: Delta had the shelf, Sungrow the power electronics, Infineon the silicon, and the grid tier the transformers. Megmeet is the one challenger whose own filings now show the transition paying — in power products, at the rack — while its hall-edge ambition stays an option. Zhonhen and Sinexcel remain the vendors whose filings disclose the least against the thesis they are valued on.

Megmeet's, Zhonhen's and Sinexcel's items rest substantially on Chinese-language exchange filings and investor-relations records read in the original. The most consequential Megmeet fact here is a negative — no service-voltage class, order figure, customer name or AI-data-centre revenue line appears in them — and a negative finding, however wide the search, is weaker evidence than a positive one.

Sinexcel's 800 VDC roadmap is sourced to an investor-relations activity record served from a third-party document host, because the SZSE origin was unreachable from the research egress. The document is company-authored and company-numbered, but its provenance tier reflects the delivery host rather than the origin.

Twelve of the fifteen dossiers carried from the 8 September edition are unchanged, and power-electronics is pinned at its 6 September v1; and this report is silent on anything that entered the public record after each pin's lastUpdated date — the oldest is 4 September 2026. The Zhonhen and Sinexcel dossiers (8 September) predate any Q3 information.

guidanceOverlays.title: Which architectures the covered vendors can actually serve today
ps: **The four deployment architectures map unevenly onto the covered roster.** The AC-baseline and retrofit options are served by everyone in the rack layer. The sidecar option is where Megmeet publishes the most complete mainland chain — a sidecar rectifying a building's existing 380–480 VAC to 800 VDC at over 1 MW per rack, with a 570 kW side rack combining BBU and PCS functions — and its power-products segment grew 60.92% in H1 2026 on an expanding margin, though no AI-data-centre revenue line is disclosed at any granularity.

**For the native-800 VDC option, one covered vendor states in a filing that the device is supplying the market — and its own curve puts volume in 2027.** Sungrow's H1 2026 interim describes its EnerNeo solid-state transformer as launched and supplying at 10–13.8 kV MVAC to 800 V DC, while its commercialisation guidance is small-batch trials through 2026 and batch orders from 2027. Megmeet's converter is in pre-research with no published input class; Sinexcel's management describes its AIDC products as samples with no formal sales. When a customer asks who can supply the native architecture now, the answer is one vendor, on paper, in trial quantities.

guidanceOverlays.title: The Panama name-check, one year on
ps: **The paper names an architecture, not a company — and the covered vendor most associated with that architecture has disclosed nothing against it.** Zhonhen's own H1 2026 interim restates the Panama product matrix (10 kV directly to 240/400/800 V DC in a single stage, over 97.5% efficiency, 2.5 MW of IT load per system) and then contains no order, no backlog, no named customer, no capacity commitment, and no occurrence of the words NVIDIA, SST or transformer-rectifier across 187 pages. Treat the name-check as validation of the device class and not as evidence of any company's pipeline.

**The TRU-now / SST-later framing has one partial exception, and it is narrower than it first read.** A covered vendor states in an exchange filing that a megawatt-class solid-state transformer is supplying the market, but the same company guides to small-batch trials through 2026 and batch orders from 2027. That does not move the 2029 date for the industry; it means a buyer asking for an SST today has one covered vendor to ask, for trial units.

guidanceOverlays.title: What the revised filings changed for supplier conversations
ps: **Separate membership from rank — and the rank is now on the record.** One covered vendor's interim claims only to be one of NVIDIA's designated recommended data-centre power suppliers, which its reply to the exchange's inquiry defines as a place on the list NVIDIA recommends to its downstream customers. The trade story that it displaced the incumbent second source traces to early-2025 pieces that call it rumour; the company says it was late on GB200 and won GB300 batch orders, and 2026 broker research expects it to be the third NVL72 PSU source. In a customer conversation, membership and third source are defensible; second is not.

**Published capability and disclosed commerce diverged measurably this half, and the filings are the place to check.** Across the three Chinese A-share vendors in the conversion layer, the interims disclose: no order, no backlog and no named customer in one case; no AI-data-centre revenue line in the second; and an explicit management statement of samples-in-development-no-formal-sales in the third. That is not a reason to discount any of them, but it does mean a supplier claim sourced to a product page or a partner roster should be checked against the most recent filing before it is repeated.

**Scale does not rank this chain.** The whole-company revenue spread across the covered roster runs from roughly USD 0.3bn to USD 45bn, and the ordering bears almost no relation to position in the 800 VDC transition — the vendor with arguably the most defensible economics in the report is among the three smallest, because it enforced patents rather than won volume.
